{{Short description|Mathematical relation in spherical triangles}}
In [[spherical trigonometry]], the '''law of cosines''' (or, more specifically, the '''law of cosines for sides'''<ref name=VNR/>) is a theorem relating the three sides and one of the angles of a [[spherical triangle]], analogous to the [[law of cosines|planar law of cosines]] for a triangle in the [[Euclidean plane]].

[[Image:Law-of-haversines.svg|right|thumb|Spherical triangle solved by the law of cosines.]]
A ''spherical triangle'' is a shape on a [[sphere]] consisting of three ''vertices'' (corner [[point (geometry)|point]]s) connected by three sides, each of which is part of a ''[[great circle]]'', the analog on the sphere of a [[straight line]] in the plane (for example the [[equator]] and [[meridian (geography)|meridian]]s of a globe). The arc lengths of the sides are proportional to the measures of the [[central angle]]s they [[subtend]]. The angles between sides are [[dihedral angle]]s between the [[Plane (geometry)|plane]]s containing them. In the image, {{math|'''u'''}}, {{math|'''v'''}}, and {{math|'''w'''}} represent three points on the sphere.  If the angular lengths of the sides are {{math|''a''}} (from {{math|'''u'''}} to {{math|'''v'''), ''b''}} (from {{math|'''u'''}} to {{math|'''w'''}}), and {{math|''c''}} (from {{math|'''v'''}} to {{math|'''w'''}}), and the angle of the corner opposite {{math|''c''}} is {{math|''C''}}, then the (first) spherical law of cosines states:<ref name=Ireneus>Romuald Ireneus 'Scibor-Marchocki, [https://web.archive.org/web/19991010004728/http://www.geocities.com/ResearchTriangle/2363/trig02.html Spherical trigonometry], ''Elementary-Geometry Trigonometry'' web page (1997).</ref><ref name=VNR>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Spherical Trigonometry |editor1=W. Gellert |editor2= H. Küstner |editor3=M. Hellwich |editor4=H. Kästner |encyclopedia=The VNR Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics |year=1975 |at=§ 1.12, {{pgs|261–282}} |publisher=Van Nostrand Reinhold}}</ref>
<math display="block">\cos c = \cos a \cos b + \sin a \sin b \cos C\,</math>

As a special case, when {{math|''C'' {{=}} {{sfrac|π|2}}}} then {{math|cos ''C'' {{=}} 0}}, resulting in the spherical analogue of the [[Pythagorean theorem]]:
<math display="block">\cos c = \cos a \cos b\,</math>

If the law of cosines is used to solve for {{math|''c''}}, the necessity of inverting the cosine magnifies [[rounding error]]s when {{math|''c''}} is small.  In this case, the alternative formulation of the [[law of haversines]] is preferable.<ref>R. W. Sinnott, "Virtues of the Haversine", Sky and Telescope 68 (2), 159 (1984).</ref>

A second spherical law of cosines, sometimes called the '''law of cosines for angles''',<ref name=VNR/> relates the three angles and one of the sides of a triangle:<ref>{{Cite book| last=Reiman | first=István | year=1999 | title=Geometria és határterületei | publisher=Szalay Könyvkiadó és Kereskedőház Kft. | page=83 }}</ref>
<math display="block">\cos C = -\cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B \cos c\,</math>
where {{math|''A''}} and {{math|''B''}} are the angles of the corners opposite to sides {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}}, respectively. It is related to the first law by [[polar duality]].

==Proofs==
===First proof===
Let {{math|'''u''', '''v'''}}, and {{math|'''w'''}} denote the [[unit vector]]s from the center of a unit sphere to those corners of the triangle.  The angles and distances do not change if the coordinate system is rotated, so we can rotate the coordinate system so that <math>\mathbf{u}</math> is at the [[north pole]] and <math>\mathbf{v}</math> is somewhere on the [[prime meridian]] (longitude of 0).  With this rotation, the [[spherical coordinates]] for <math>\mathbf{v}</math> are <math>(r, \theta, \phi) = (1, a, 0) ,</math> where {{mvar|θ}} is the angle measured from the north pole not from the equator, and the spherical coordinates for <math>\mathbf{w}</math> are <math>(r, \theta, \phi) = (1, b, C) .</math>  The [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]] for <math>\mathbf{v}</math> are <math>(x, y, z) = (\sin a, 0, \cos a)</math> and the Cartesian coordinates for <math>\mathbf{w}</math> are <math>(x, y, z) = (\sin b \cos C, \sin b \sin C, \cos b) .</math>  The value of <math>\cos c</math> is the dot product of the two Cartesian vectors, which is <math>\sin a \sin b \cos C + \cos a \cos b .</math>

===Second proof===
Let {{math|'''u''', '''v'''}}, and {{math|'''w'''}} denote the [[unit vector]]s from the center of the sphere to those corners of the triangle.  We have {{math|1='''u''' · '''u''' = 1}}, {{math|1='''v''' · '''w''' = cos ''c''}}, {{math|1='''u''' · '''v''' = cos ''a''}}, and {{math|1='''u''' · '''w''' = cos ''b''}}.  The vectors {{math|'''u''' × '''v'''}} and {{math|'''u''' × '''w'''}} have lengths {{math|sin ''a''}} and {{math|sin ''b''}} respectively and the angle between them is {{math|''C''}}, so
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \sin a \sin b \cos C &= (\bold u \times \bold v) \cdot (\bold u \times \bold w) \\
  &= (\bold u \cdot \bold u)(\bold v \cdot \bold w) - (\bold u \cdot \bold w)(\bold v \cdot \bold u) \\
  &= \cos c - \cos a \cos b
\end{align}</math>
using [[cross product]]s, [[dot product]]s, and the [[Binet–Cauchy identity]] 
<math display=block>
(\bold p \times \bold q) \cdot (\bold r \times \bold s) = (\bold p \cdot \bold r)(\bold q \cdot \bold s) - (\bold p \cdot \bold s)(\bold q \cdot \bold r).</math>

===Third proof===
There is a proof using [[quaternion]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Brand |first=Louis |title=Vector and Tensor Analysis |year=1947 |publisher=Wiley |pages=416–417 |chapter=§186 Great Circle Arccs |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/vectortensoranal00branrich/page/416/ }}</ref> Let {{math|'''u'''}}, {{math|'''v'''}}, and {{math|'''w'''}} denote the [[unit vector]]s from the center of the unit sphere to those corners of the triangle. We define the quaternion {{math|1=''u'' = (0, '''u''') = 0 + ''u''{{sub|''x''}}'''i''' + ''u''{{sub|''y''}}'''j''' + ''u''{{sub|''z''}}'''k'''}}.  The quaternion {{mvar|u}} is used to represent a rotation by 180° around the axis indicated by the vector {{math|'''u'''}}.  We note that using {{math|−'''u'''}} as the axis of rotation gives the same result, and that the rotation is its own inverse.  We also define {{math|1=''v'' = (0, '''v''')}} and {{math|1=''w'' = (0, '''w''')}}.

We compute the [[Hamilton product|product of quaternions]], which also gives the composition of the corresponding rotations:
<math display="block">
q = vu^{-1} = (v)(-u) = (-(\bold v \cdot -\bold u), \bold v \times -\bold u) = (\bold u \cdot \bold v, \bold u \times \bold v) = (\cos a, \bold w' \sin a)
</math>
where {{math|(''f'', '''g''')}} represents the real (scalar) and imaginary (vector) parts of a quaternion, {{mvar|a}} is the angle between {{math|'''u'''}} and {{math|'''v'''}}, and {{math|1='''w'''′ = ('''u''' × '''v''') / {{abs|'''u''' × '''v'''}}}} is the axis of the rotation that moves {{math|'''u'''}} to {{math|'''v'''}} along a great circle.  Similarly we define:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
r &= wv^{-1} = (\bold v \cdot \bold w, \bold v \times \bold w) = (\cos c, \bold u' \sin c) \\
s &= uw^{-1} = (\bold w \cdot \bold u, \bold w \times \bold u) = (\cos b, \bold v' \sin b). \\
\end{align}</math>

The quaternions {{mvar|q}}, {{mvar|r}}, and {{mvar|s}} are used to represent rotations with axes of rotation {{math|'''w'''′}}, {{math|'''u'''′}}, and {{math|'''v'''′}}, respectively, and angles of rotation {{math|2''a''}}, {{math|2''b''}}, and {{math|2''c''}}, respectively.  (Because these are double angles, each of {{mvar|q}}, {{mvar|r}}, and {{mvar|s}} represents two applications of the rotation implied by an edge of the spherical triangle.)

From the definitions, it follows that
<math display="block">qsr = vu^{-1}uw^{-1}wv^{-1} = 1,</math>
which tells us that the composition of these rotations is the identity transformation.  In particular, {{math|1=''qs'' = ''r''{{sup|−1}}}} gives us
<math display="block">(\cos a, \bold w' \sin a) (\cos b, \bold v' \sin b) = (\cos c, -\bold u' \sin c).</math>

Expanding the left-hand side, we obtain 
<math display="block">(\cos a \cos b - \bold w' \cdot \bold v' \sin a \sin b, \bold w' \cos a \sin b + \bold v' \sin a \cos b  + \bold w' \times \bold v' \sin a \sin b). </math>

Equating the real parts on both sides of the identity, we obtain
<math display="block">\cos a \cos b - \bold w' \cdot \bold v' \sin a \sin b = \cos c.</math>

Because {{math|'''w'''′}} is parallel to {{math|'''u''' × '''v'''}}, {{math|'''v'''′}} is parallel to {{math|1='''w''' × '''u''' = −'''u''' × '''w'''}}, and {{mvar|C}} is the angle between {{math|'''u''' × '''v'''}} and {{math|'''u''' × '''w'''}}, it follows that <math>\bold w' \cdot \bold v' = -\cos C</math>. Thus,
<math display="block">\cos a \cos b + \cos C \sin a \sin b = \cos c.</math>

==Rearrangements==
The first and second spherical laws of cosines can be rearranged to put the sides ({{math|''a'', ''b'', ''c''}}) and angles ({{math|''A'', ''B'', ''C''}}) on opposite sides of the equations:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\cos C &= \frac{\cos c - \cos a \cos b}{\sin a \sin b} \\
\cos c &= \frac{\cos C + \cos A \cos B}{\sin A \sin B} \\
\end{align}</math>

== Planar limit: small angles ==
For ''small'' spherical triangles, i.e. for small {{math|''a'', ''b''}}, and {{math|''c''}}, the spherical law of cosines is approximately the same as the ordinary planar law of cosines,
<math display="block">c^2 \approx a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C \,.</math>

To prove this, we will use the [[small-angle approximation]] obtained from the [[Maclaurin series]] for the cosine and sine functions:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \cos a &= 1 - \frac{a^2}{2} + O\left(a^4\right) \\
  \sin a &= a + O\left(a^3\right)
\end{align}</math>

Substituting these expressions into the spherical law of cosines nets:
<math display="block">
  1 - \frac{c^2}{2} + O\left(c^4\right) =
  1 - \frac{a^2}{2} - \frac{b^2}{2} + \frac{a^2 b^2}{4} + O\left(a^4\right) + O\left(b^4\right) + \cos(C)\left(ab + O\left(a^3 b\right) + O\left(ab^3\right) + O\left(a^3 b^3\right)\right)
</math>
or after simplifying:
<math display="block">c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C + O\left(c^4\right) + O\left(a^4\right) + O\left(b^4\right) + O\left(a^2 b^2\right) + O\left(a^3 b\right) + O\left(ab^3\right) + O\left(a^3 b^3\right).</math>

The [[big O notation|big O]] terms for {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} are dominated by {{math|''O''(''a''<sup>4</sup>) + ''O''(''b''<sup>4</sup>)}} as {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} get small, so we can write this last expression as:
<math display="block">c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C + O\left(a^4\right) + O\left(b^4\right) + O\left(c^4\right).</math>
== History ==
Various trigonometric equations equivalent to the spherical law of cosines were used in the course of solving astronomical problems by medieval Islamic astronomers [[Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi|al-Khwārizmī]] (9th century) and [[al-Battani|al-Battānī]] (c. 900), Indian astronomer [[Nilakantha Somayaji|Nīlakaṇṭha]] (15th century), and Austrian astronomer [[Georg von Peuerbach]] (15th century) but none of them treated it as a general method for solving spherical triangles.<ref>{{cite book |last=Van Brummelen |first=Glen |year=2012 |title=Heavenly mathematics: The forgotten art of spherical trigonometry |publisher=Princeton University Press |page=98|bibcode=2012hmfa.book.....V }}</ref> For example, al-Khwārizmī calculated the azimuth {{tmath|\alpha}} of the Sun in terms of its altitude {{tmath|h}}, terrestrial latitude {{tmath|\phi}}, and ortive amplitude {{tmath|\psi}} ([[angular distance]] between due East and the Sun's rising place on the horizon) as {{tmath|1= \cos \alpha = (\sin\psi - \tan\phi \sin h)/\cos h}}.{{sfn|Van Brummelen|2009|at="Early Spherical Astronomy: Graphical Methods and Analemmas", § 4.7, {{pgs|166–172}} }} (See [[Horizontal coordinate system]].)

The spherical law of cosines appeared as an independent trigonometrical identity for solving spherical triangles in Peuerbach's student [[Regiomontanus]]'s {{lang|la|De triangulis omnimodis}} (unfinished at Regiomontanus's death in 1476, published posthumously 1533), a foundational work for European trigonometry and astronomy which comprehensively described how to solve plane and spherical triangles. Regiomontanus used nearly the modern form, but written in terms of the [[versine]], {{tmath|1= \operatorname{vers} x = 1 - \cos x}}, rather than the cosine,{{sfn|Van Brummelen|2009|at="From Ptolemy to Triangles: John of Gmunden, Peurbach, Regiomontanus", § 6.5, {{pgs|247–263}}}}
<math display="block">\frac{\operatorname{vers} C}{\operatorname{vers} c - \operatorname{vers}(a-b)} = \frac{1}{\sin a \sin b}.</math>

Mathematical historians have speculated that Regiomontanus may have adapted the result from specific astronomical examples in al-Battānī's {{transliteration|ar|Kitāb az-Zīj aṣ-Ṣābi’}}, which was published in Latin translation annotated by Regiomontanus in 1537.{{sfn|Van Brummelen|2009|page=260}}
